title: I am a person who studies.
dek: “I want good grades” gets checked a few times a year. “I am a person who studies” gets checked every evening, and that changes what one bad day costs.
whyThisIdea: Este primul subiect nefolosit din backlog și continuă firul săptămânii (studiatul cu cartea închisă, telefonul în altă cameră): testează pe școală argumentul identitate vs rezultat din recenzia Atomic Habits, cu un studiu verificabil și un calcul simplu de „voturi” până la sfârșit de an.

entry.title: I am a person who studies.
entry.titleHtml: I am a person who studies.
entry.dek: “I want good grades” gets checked a few times a year. “I am a person who studies” gets checked every evening, and that changes what one bad day costs.
body: “Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become.” — James Clear

Have you ever asked yourself what you actually answer when somebody asks why you study? Mine was always the same, and I never thought about it: “I want good grades.” In the last two articles I tried to study with the book closed, then I put the phone in another room, and somewhere between those two experiments I noticed that the sentence underneath all of it was never the method. It was that answer. So the question is: what if the reason you give for studying is part of the reason it is so hard? Let’s start from the beginning.

In the Atomic Habits review, back in September, I wrote about the three layers James Clear puts around every habit: the outcome on the outside, the process in the middle, and the identity in the centre. I explained it with the gym and the 10 kg, because that is the example everybody uses. But I am a student, and the place where I spend most of my hours is not the gym, it is the desk. And “I want good grades” is about the purest outcome sentence there is. So today I want to test the argument where it matters most for me.

Firstly, let’s put the two sentences next to each other, the way I like to split a title. “I want good grades” starts with want, which means it is about something you do not have yet, and it ends with a thing that somebody else decides, on one day, a few times a year. “I am a person who studies” starts with I am, it is about today, and the only person who can check it is you. An outcome gets checked on the day of the test. An identity gets checked every evening. This is what Clear means when he says every action is a vote. Nobody becomes a person who studies in one night, but every night you either add a vote or you don’t.

Secondly, let’s count the votes, because I think the number changes how a bad day feels. Today is Tuesday, the 3rd of November, and there are 59 days left until the end of the year.
Days from today to the 31st of December: 59
Weekdays in those 59 days: 43
Say I skip every Friday, and there are 8 Fridays left: 43 - 8 = 35 votes out of 43, so 81%
That is a very clear majority, and I did not need a perfect week once. Now look at what “I want good grades” does with the same two months. On all the evenings without a test it has nothing to say, so skipping one feels free. And on the day the grade comes, one bad result feels like a verdict on the whole thing. The outcome sentence makes every normal evening worthless and every bad test final. The identity sentence makes every evening count and no single one decisive.

Thirdly, the part that made me take this seriously, because I wanted to know if it is more than a nice way of talking. In 2011, four psychologists, Christopher Bryan, Gregory Walton, Todd Rogers and Carol Dweck, published a study called “Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self”. Just before the 2008 presidential election, 88 registered voters in California filled in a short survey. For half of them the questions talked about voting. For the other half, the same questions talked about being a voter. That was the whole difference. Then the researchers checked the official records to see who really voted.
“Voting” group: 81.8% voted
“Being a voter” group: 95.5% voted
That is 13.7 points, from changing a verb into a noun. They repeated it in New Jersey in 2009 and got 79.0% against 89.9%, almost 11 points.

Why would one word do that? I think it is because a verb is something you do on a day, and a noun is something you are. Skipping a verb costs you nothing, it is just one day. Skipping a noun costs you a little bit of who you said you were. Put it in school terms: “I want good grades” lets you skip tonight, because tonight does not decide the grade. <u>“I am a person who studies” does not let you skip tonight for free, because tonight is the only place that sentence can be true.</u>

But there is a trap here, and I fell into it before. If “a person who studies” turns into “a person who sits at the desk for four hours”, then the identity is just the look of studying. On Sunday I wrote that the hours are not the learning, and that still stands. So the identity has to be defined by the real thing, not the costume. For me, a person who studies is a person who closes the book and tries to write down what is in it, even when the page comes out half empty.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. On a piece of paper I am drawing 43 boxes, one for every weekday from today to the 31st of December. A box gets marked only if that evening I closed the book and tried to remember, no matter for how long and no matter how badly it went. I am not writing down any grade on that paper. At the end of the year I will count the boxes, and that number will tell me more about who I am as a student than anything on a report card.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the idea is right, and I can already feel the difference between the two sentences in my own head. But I have to be fair about the evidence. In 2016 a much bigger replication, by Alan Gerber and his colleagues, tried the same noun versus verb trick and found no real difference in turnout, so I would not build everything on one word in one survey. I also think “I am a person who studies” can feel like a small lie on the first day, when you have not done anything yet. And grades do matter - they decide schools and scholarships, and pretending they don’t would be dishonest. What I take from it is smaller: the grade is the scoreboard, but the person who studies is the one who plays.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become.” — James Clear
